en: In the City of Destruction, a man sat reading a Book. The more he read, the heavier his heart grew.
This Book says our city will be burned with fire from heaven. What shall I do to be saved?
And this burden on my back grows heavier every day.
You are tired, that is all. Sleep, and you will feel better in the morning.
Stay with them, or go?
Stay and hope the city improves
Leave and find the way
He dreamed of red smoke over the rooftops. When he woke, the burden was heavier still.
Flee from the wrath to come.
There goes the man with the Book again.
He has gone soft in the head, poor fellow.
Neighbour, where are you going? Come back with us!
I am going to an inheritance that cannot fade away. Come with me.
Tush! Away with your Book. Will you come back with us or no?
No, not I. I have laid my hand to the plough.
Come, Pliable, let us go home. I will not keep company with such a fool.
Wait. If what he says is true, things are better where he is going. I will go with him.
Then you are both fools. I am going home.
Tell me more of the place we are going. Is it truly so good?
There is a kingdom there that will never end, and crowns of glory for those who reach it.
Why are you crying?
Sir, I read that I am condemned to die and after that to come to judgement. I am not ready.
Then why do you stand still?
Because I do not know which way to go.
Do you see yonder wicket gate?
No.
Do you see yonder shining light?
I think I do.
Keep that light in your eye, and go straight toward it. There you will find the gate. Knock, and you will be told what to do.
Read the Book when you are unsure of the way. It will show you what you cannot see.
So he began to run, crying, 'Life, life, eternal life!'

The Slough of Despond
Christian and Pliable went on together across the plain, talking of the country ahead.
Come, let us mend our pace. I long to see those crowns and robes.
Keep moving in the mire, or it will hold you fast.
Being heedless, they both fell suddenly into the bog. Christian, because of the burden on his back, began to sink.
Is this the happiness you have told me of all this while?
If I get out again with my life, you shall have the brave country alone for me.
With that, Pliable struggled out of the mire on the side nearest his own house, and Christian saw him no more.
By order of the Lawgiver, good and firm steps are set through the very midst of this slough.
Do not look at the mire. Look for the steps.
What are you doing there?
Sir, I was told to go this way to the gate. Fear followed me so hard that I fled the nearest way, and fell in.
But why did you not look for the steps? Give me your hand.
This slough cannot be mended. When a man wakes to his sin, his fears and doubts run down and settle here. That is why it is called Despond.
So Help set him upon sound ground, and bid him go on his way.
The Wicket Gate
Christian walked on alone. Across the field a gentleman came to meet him. His name was Mr Worldly Wiseman.
How now, good fellow, where are you going in this burdened manner?
A burdened manner indeed. I am going to yonder wicket gate, where I am told I shall be rid of it.
In the village of Morality lives a gentleman named Legality. He can take off such burdens, and the road to his house is smooth.
Which way?
Take the smooth road to Morality
Keep to the narrow way
The hill hung over the road. Flashes of fire came out of it, and Christian was afraid it would fall on his head.
What are you doing here, Christian?
Did I not show you the way to the little wicket gate? Mr Legality cannot set you free from your burden.
Sir, I am sorry. May I yet go back and up to the gate?
The man at the gate will receive you, for he has goodwill for men. Only take heed that you turn not aside again.
Strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life.
Arrows fly from the castle beyond the wall. When you see the glint, shelter behind a rock.
May I now enter here? Will he within open to sorry me, though I have been an undeserving rebel?
Who is there? Where do you come from, and what would you have?
I am willing with all my heart. We make no objections against any.
As Christian stepped in, Goodwill gave him a pull, for arrows fly from that castle at all who come up to this gate.
The Interpreter's House
Christian came to the house of the Interpreter, and knocked over and over.
Come in. I will show you that which will be profitable to you.
A large parlour, full of dust, because it was never swept.
He began to sweep, and the dust flew about so that it almost choked him.
Bring water, and sprinkle the room.
Christian took up the jug of water.
The water laid the dust, and the room was swept and cleansed with pleasure.
The dust is too thick. I need something to settle it.
The dust is sin. The broom is the Law, which only stirs it up. The water is the Gospel, which lays it down.
One stands by the fire, always casting water on it, yet the fire burns higher and hotter.
Behind the wall stood a man with a vessel of oil, secretly casting it into the fire.
This is Christ, who with the oil of his grace keeps alive the work already begun in the heart.
Salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks.
Up this way ran Christian, but not without great difficulty, because of the load on his back.
Just as Christian came up to the Cross, his burden loosed from his shoulders and fell from his back. It tumbled till it came to the mouth of the sepulchre, where it fell in, and was seen no more.
He has given me rest by his sorrow, and life by his death.
Your sins are forgiven.
Put off your rags. Here is a change of clothes.
Take this Roll with its seal. Look on it as you run, and give it in at the Celestial Gate.
Then Christian gave three leaps for joy, and went on singing.
Free of the burden, you can jump again in the air.
